content.title: Concavity and Inflection Points
content.overview: This lesson focuses on using the second derivative to determine the concavity of a function and identifying points of inflection. It emphasizes the necessity of a sign change in the second derivative to justify the existence of an inflection point.
learning_objectives: Identify intervals where a function is concave up or concave down using the second derivative.
Locate candidate points for inflection where the second derivative is zero or undefined.
Justify the existence of an inflection point by verifying a change in concavity across a point in the domain.

sections.title: Defining Concavity
sections.content: Concavity describes the 'bend' of a curve. A function $f$ is concave up on an interval if its derivative $f'$ is increasing, which corresponds to $f''(x) > 0$. Visually, the graph lies above its tangent lines. Conversely, $f$ is concave down on an interval if $f'$ is decreasing, which corresponds to $f''(x) < 0$. In this case, the graph lies below its tangent lines.

sections.title: Identifying Inflection Points
sections.content: An inflection point is a point on the graph of a continuous function where the concavity changes from concave up to concave down, or vice versa. To find these points, first identify values of $x$ in the domain where $f''(x) = 0$ or $f''(x)$ is undefined. These are 'candidates.' A candidate only becomes an inflection point if the sign of $f''(x)$ actually changes as you pass through that $x$-value.

sections.title: The Sign-Change Test
sections.content:
To justify an inflection point, you must perform a sign-change test. 1. Find all $x$ where $f''(x) = 0$ or is undefined. 2. Test the sign of $f''(x)$ on the intervals created by these points. 3. If $f''(x)$ changes from positive to negative (or negative to positive) at $x=c$, and $f$ is continuous at $c$, then $(c, f(c))$ is an inflection point. If the sign does not change, it is not an inflection point, even if $f''(c) = 0$.

![A linear sequence showing the steps to identify an inflection point: Find f double prime, locate zeros or undefined points, test signs on intervals, and confirm sign change.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/f49071a7-5da7-4e0d-9180-b664ceca6a78-1786519360652-895.webp)

worked_examples.question: Let $f$ be a twice-differentiable function. A table of values for $f''(x)$ is provided: $f''(1) = -2$, $f''(2) = 0$, and $f''(3) = 5$. Determine if $x=2$ is an inflection point and justify your answer.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Identify the candidate. $f''(2) = 0$, so $x=2$ is a candidate for an inflection point. Step 2: Check signs around the candidate. To the left at $x=1$, $f''(1) = -2$ (negative), so $f$ is concave down. To the right at $x=3$, $f''(3) = 5$ (positive), so $f$ is concave up. Step 3: Conclusion. Because $f$ is twice-differentiable (implying continuity) and the sign of $f''(x)$ changes from negative to positive at $x=2$, $x=2$ is an inflection point.

common_mistakes: Assuming $f''(x) = 0$ automatically means there is an inflection point. (Example: $f(x) = x^4$ has $f''(0) = 0$ but no inflection point because it is concave up on both sides).
Forgetting to check if the function is defined/continuous at the point where $f''(x)$ is undefined.
Confusing the sign of $f'(x)$ (increasing/decreasing) with the sign of $f''(x)$ (concavity).
exam_tips: Always state that $f''(x)$ changes sign in your written justification; simply saying $f''(x)=0$ will not earn full credit.
If $f''$ is not given, look at the behavior of $f'$. If $f'$ is increasing, $f$ is concave up. If $f'$ is decreasing, $f$ is concave down.
Check the domain. A point where $f''$ is undefined can only be an inflection point if the original function $f$ is defined there.
content.recap: Concavity is determined by the sign of the second derivative ($f''$). An inflection point occurs where a continuous function changes concavity, requiring $f''$ to change sign. Finding $f''(x)=0$ is only the first step; the sign-change test is the required justification.

knowledge_claims.content: A function $f$ is concave up on an interval if $f''(x) > 0$ for all $x$ in that interval.
A function $f$ is concave down on an interval if $f''(x) < 0$ for all $x$ in that interval.
If the first derivative $f'$ is increasing on an interval, then the function $f$ is concave up on that interval.
If the first derivative $f'$ is decreasing on an interval, then the function $f$ is concave down on that interval.
An inflection point is a point where a function is continuous and its concavity changes from up to down or down to up.
To find candidate inflection points, solve for $x$ where $f''(x) = 0$ or where $f''(x)$ does not exist.
It is a mistake to conclude an inflection point exists solely because $f''(x) = 0$ without verifying a sign change.
A point where $f''(x)$ is undefined can be an inflection point only if the function $f$ is continuous at that point.
A change in the sign of $f''(x)$ from positive to negative indicates a transition from concave up to concave down.
If $f''(x)$ is positive on both sides of a point where $f''(x) = 0$, no inflection point occurs at that $x$ value.
On a graph of $f$, an inflection point is where the curve switches from being 'bowl-shaped' to 'umbrella-shaped' or vice versa.
While relative extrema are related to the first derivative's sign changes, inflection points are related to the second derivative's sign changes.

items.stem: Which procedure or value is mathematically consistent in “AP Calculus BC — Concavity and Inflection Points — Practice Record 01”?

options.A: Concavity and Inflection Points: The sign of the second derivative determines concavity, and an inflection point requires an actual change in concavity.
options.B: Improper Integrals: An improper integral is defined by a limit at an infinite bound or unbounded integrand and converges only when that limit is finite.
options.C: Area Between Curves: Area between curves integrates top minus bottom or right minus left after locating relevant intersections and interval changes.
options.D: Polar Coordinates and Derivatives: Polar points use radius and angle, and polar slope follows from parametric differentiation of x=r cos theta and y=r sin theta.

items.explanation: Choice A is best because The sign of the second derivative determines concavity, and an inflection point requires an actual change in concavity. The other options invoke different atomic topics and do not satisfy the record's stated target as directly.

items.stem: Which relationship connects the verbal and symbolic information in “AP Calculus BC — Concavity and Inflection Points — Practice Record 02”?

options.A: Slope Fields and Solution Curves: A slope field displays the derivative prescribed at each point, and solution curves must follow those local slopes without crossing incompatible directions.
options.B: Concavity and Inflection Points: The sign of the second derivative determines concavity, and an inflection point requires an actual change in concavity.
options.C: Volumes with Cross Sections: A solid with known cross-sectional area has volume equal to the integral of that area along the perpendicular axis.
options.D: Polar Area: Polar area over an angular interval is one half the integral of the squared radius, with intersections determining correct angular bounds.

items.explanation: Choice B is best because The sign of the second derivative determines concavity, and an inflection point requires an actual change in concavity. The other options invoke different atomic topics and do not satisfy the record's stated target as directly.
